name: Tipping Point and Atomic-Network Replication

positioning.oneLineSummary: Tests whether successful atomic networks can be reproduced with improving cost, speed, retention, and reduced manual support.
positioning.productLabel: Tipping-Point Replication — based on Andrew Chen's public Cold Start materials

attribution.display: Based on Andrew Chen's public Cold Start materials

neutralParaphrase: After one atomic network works, evaluate whether the company can create many more. Compare time, cost, hard-side acquisition, density, retention, and subsidy by launch cohort; recognize that each city, team, or segment may restart the cold-start problem.

locator.value: Local network effects reset by geography and atomic-unit metrics

requiredConditions: At least one stable atomic network is evidenced.
New network launches can be identified as cohorts.
Launch support and subsidy are measured.

requiredEvidence.description: Unit-level launch date, hard-side seed, spend, manual work, time to density, retention, and outcomes.
Repeatable launch sequence, owner, channels, norms, and stop criteria.
Differences across geography, segment, density, culture, regulation, or hard-side supply.

decisionQuestions: How many atomic networks reached stable value?
Are time, cost, subsidy, and manual effort improving by cohort?
Which local attributes explain success or failure?
What part of the playbook transfers and what resets?
positiveSignals: Several independent units cross a pre-registered operating threshold.
Time and cost to density improve without weaker retention.
Failed units produce clear boundary conditions.
redFlags: One flagship city or team represents all scalability.
Later cohorts receive hidden higher subsidy.
Aggregate growth masks failed local launches.
disconfirmingEvidence: New units do not retain after launch teams leave.
Cost or subsidy rises with expansion.
Success depends on a nonreplicable local partnership.
New markets require a different hard side or interaction.
contraindications: Do not call global scale before local replication is shown.
Do not average unit outcomes without dispersion.
Do not assume adjacent geography or vertical shares the same threshold.

instructions: Define unit-level success before comparing cohorts.
Calculate time, cost, subsidy, density, and retention per launch.
Separate repeatable playbook from local exception.
Conclude replicating, partially replicating, nonreplicable, or insufficient data.

deterministicRule.prohibition: The language model must not calculate or redefine success thresholds.

sourceReliability.high: Complete unit-level spend, operations, interaction, and retention data.

evidenceStrength.medium: Multiple units work but efficiency is flat or mixed.
evidenceStrength.high: Repeated units work with stable or improving economics.

evidenceCoverage.medium: Density and retention covered; cost or failures partial.
evidenceCoverage.high: Launch, hard side, cost, subsidy, density, retention, failures, and local context complete.

applicabilityConfidence.medium: Initial unit exists but expansion is early.

judgmentConfidence.high: A repeatable and economically improving launch system is evidenced.

empiricalQualifications: Expansion cohorts are selected and environment-dependent.
Learning curves may reverse as easy markets are exhausted.

rights.notes: Public book and affiliated metric concepts are neutrally paraphrased.

openIssues: Define comparable-cohort rules for different network archetypes.
